java-oop.tldr:
• Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism (overloading at compile time, overriding at runtime).
  • Equal objects must have equal hash codes: override equals and hashCode together, or use a record.
  • Abstract classes share state and code; interfaces define capabilities and allow multiple inheritance.
  • Java is always pass-by-value; for objects the reference is copied. Prefer composition over inheritance.
java-oop.body:
Object-oriented design organizes code around objects that own their data and behaviour. The four pillars, with what each actually buys you:

Pillar Meaning Java mechanism What it buys
Encapsulation hide state; expose behaviour private fields, methods that enforce invariants you can change internals without breaking callers; invariants can't be bypassed
Abstraction expose what, hide how interfaces, abstract classes callers depend on a contract, not an implementation
Inheritance reuse and specialize via "is-a" extends, implements shared behaviour; substitutability
Polymorphism one call, many behaviours overriding (runtime), overloading (compile time) new types plug in without changing callers

Polymorphism at runtime — dynamic dispatch

Checkout calls method.charge(...); which implementation runs is decided at runtime from the object's actual class (via the class's virtual method table). Adding NetBankingPayment needs no change to Checkout — that's the open/closed principle in practice.

Overloading vs overriding

Overloading Overriding
Same name, different parameter lists same signature in a subclass
Resolved at compile time from the static types of arguments at runtime from the dynamic type of the receiver
Return type can differ same or covariant (a subtype)
Access any can't be more restrictive
Exceptions any can't throw broader checked exceptions
static / private methods can be overloaded can't be overridden (static ones are hidden)
Java
class Printer {
    void print(Object o) { System.out.println("object"); }
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("string"); }
}
Object x = "hello";
new Printer().print(x);   // prints "object": overload chosen from the static type Object at compile time

The equals / hashCode contract — the most asked question in Java interviews.

  • equals must be reflexive (a.equals(a)), symmetric, transitive, consistent, and a.equals(null) is false.
  • Equal objects must have equal hash codes. Unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision), which only costs performance.
  • Override both or neither.

If two "equal" keys have different hash codes, get looks in the wrong bucket and never even calls equals: the entry is effectively lost.

Java
public final class EmployeeId {
    private final String dept;
    private final int number;

    public EmployeeId(String dept, int number) { this.dept = dept; this.number = number; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof EmployeeId other)) return false;   // pattern matching (Java 16)
        return number == other.number && dept.equals(other.dept);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(dept, number); }
    @Override public String toString() { return dept + "-" + number; }
}
// A record generates all three: record EmployeeId(String dept, int number) {}

Pitfall mutating a field that participates in hashCode after the object is inside a HashSet/HashMap key makes it unfindable: it sits in the bucket for its old hash. Use immutable keys.

Pitfall: instanceof in equals with subclasses that add state breaks symmetry (point.equals(colorPoint) true, reverse false). Use getClass() != o.getClass() when subclasses can be equal-relevant, or make the class final.

Abstract class vs interface

Abstract class Interface
State instance fields only static final constants
Constructors yes no
Methods any, including protected abstract, default, static, private (Java 9)
Inheritance single (extends) multiple (implements A, B)
Use when closely related classes share state and code (template method) a capability across unrelated types (Comparable, AutoCloseable)

Composition over inheritance. Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent's implementation (the fragile base class problem): the classic example is extending HashSet to count additions, where overriding both add and addAll double-counts because addAll calls add internally. Composition — holding the collaborator in a field and delegating — avoids that coupling and lets you swap behaviour at runtime.

Java
// Composition: count additions without depending on HashSet's internals
public class CountingSet<E> {
    private final Set<E> delegate = new HashSet<>();
    private int added;
    public boolean add(E e) { added++; return delegate.add(e); }
    public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return delegate.addAll(c); }
    public int addedCount() { return added; }
}

Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value passed is the reference: a method can mutate the object, but reassigning the parameter doesn't affect the caller's variable.

Java
void rename(Employee e) { e.setName("new"); e = new Employee("other"); }
// caller's object now has name "new"; the caller still points to the same object, not "other"

Other object-model facts interviewers check: super() is implicitly the first statement of every constructor; constructors aren't inherited; calling overridable methods from a constructor sees a half-initialized subclass; this escaping a constructor breaks thread-safety; access levels are private < package-private < protected < public.

java-strings.tldr:
• Strings are immutable: thread-safe, cacheable hash codes, safe keys, and they enable the string pool.
  • == compares references; equals compares content; intern() returns the pooled copy.
  • Use StringBuilder for concatenation in loops; StringBuffer is the legacy synchronized version.
  • Keep passwords in char[] so they can be cleared.
java-strings.body:
String is immutable and final: once created, its characters never change. Every "modifying" method (concat, replace, toUpperCase, substring) returns a new String.

Why immutability was chosen

Benefit Why it matters
Thread safety strings can be shared across threads with no synchronization
Cached hash code hashCode() is computed once and stored, making strings fast HashMap keys
Security class names, file paths, URLs and SQL can't be changed after validation by another reference holder
String pool identical literals can safely share one object

The string pool

Java
String a = "hello";                 // literal: taken from the pool
String b = "hello";                 // same pooled object
String c = new String("hello");     // a new heap object (may also create the pooled literal)
System.out.println(a == b);         // true  (same reference)
System.out.println(a == c);         // false (different objects)
System.out.println(a.equals(c));    // true  (same content)
System.out.println(a == c.intern());// true  (intern returns the pooled copy)

String d = "hel" + "lo";            // compile-time constant folding: pooled, d == a is true
String part = "hel";
String e = part + "lo";             // computed at runtime: a new object, e == a is false
  • Since Java 7 the pool lives on the heap (not PermGen), so unused pooled strings can be garbage collected.
  • new String("x") can create up to two objects: the pooled literal (if it isn't already there) and the new heap object.
  • Compact strings (Java 9): strings containing only Latin-1 characters store 1 byte per char (byte[] + a coder flag) instead of 2, roughly halving string memory in typical apps.
  • G1 can deduplicate identical string contents (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication), sharing the backing arrays.

Concatenation: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer

String + StringBuilder StringBuffer
Mutability immutable mutable mutable
Thread-safe yes (immutable) no yes (synchronized methods)
Use simple expressions building strings in loops legacy code; rarely needed
Java
// O(n²): each += copies everything built so far
String csv = "";
for (String s : items) csv += s + ",";

// O(n): one growing buffer
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(items.size() * 16);
for (String s : items) sb.append(s).append(',');
String csv2 = sb.toString();

// Usually best: let the library do it
String csv3 = String.join(",", items);
String csv4 = items.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(",", "[", "]"));

Since Java 9, simple a + b + c expressions compile to an invokedynamic call to StringConcatFactory, which sizes the result exactly — so don't "optimize" one-line concatenations into StringBuilders. Loops are the case that matters.

Useful modern APIs: isBlank(), strip() (Unicode-aware trim), lines(), repeat(n) (Java 11); formatted(...), text blocks (Java 15); chars() / codePoints() streams.

Equality and comparison rules

  • Compare content with equals, never == (unless you deliberately compare identity).
  • "literal".equals(variable) avoids a NullPointerException when variable is null; Objects.equals(a, b) handles both.
  • equalsIgnoreCase, and compareTo for lexicographic ordering (UTF-16 code units; use Collator for human-language sorting).

Pitfall passwords and secrets belong in char[] (or byte[]), not String. You can overwrite an array after use; a String lingers in memory (and possibly the pool) until GC, and shows up in heap dumps.

Pitfall: String.split(regex) treats its argument as a regex: "a.b".split(".") returns an empty array. Use split("\\.") or Pattern.quote(".").

java-collections.tldr:
• HashMap: spread hash, bucket by hash & (n-1), chain collisions, treeify at 8 when capacity ≥ 64, resize at 0.75 load.
  • ArrayList beats LinkedList almost always; ArrayDeque is the best stack/queue.
  • Fail-fast iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException; remove with removeIf or the iterator.
  • List.of is immutable; Collections.unmodifiableList is only a read-only view.
java-collections.body:
HashMap internals (Java 8+)

  1. Hash spreading: hash = h ^ (h >>> 16) mixes the high bits of hashCode() into the low bits, because the bucket index uses only the low bits.
  2. Bucket index: index = hash & (n − 1), equivalent to hash % n because n is a power of two.
  3. Collisions go into a linked list in that bucket. Lookup walks the list comparing hashes first, then equals.
  4. Treeification: a bucket with ≥ 8 entries becomes a red-black tree (O(log n) lookups) — but only when the table has ≥ 64 buckets; with a smaller table, HashMap resizes instead. A tree shrinks back to a list at ≤ 6 entries.
  5. Resizing: when size > capacity × loadFactor (default 16 × 0.75 = 12), the table doubles. Each entry either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity, decided by a single bit of its hash — no full rehash needed.
  6. Nulls: one null key (always bucket 0) and any number of null values.
Java
// Pre-size when you know the count, to avoid repeated resizes
Map<String, User> users = HashMap.newHashMap(10_000);   // Java 19+; before: new HashMap<>((int) (10_000 / 0.75f) + 1)

Complexities

Structure get / contains add remove Notes
ArrayList O(1) by index; O(n) contains amortized O(1) at end O(n) (shifts) contiguous, cache-friendly; grows by 1.5×
LinkedList O(n) by index O(1) at ends O(1) via iterator ~40 bytes overhead per element; rarely the right choice
HashMap / HashSet O(1) average, O(log n) worst O(1) O(1) unordered
LinkedHashMap O(1) O(1) O(1) insertion or access order (basis for LRU)
TreeMap / TreeSet O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) sorted; floorKey, ceilingKey, subMap, headMap
PriorityQueue O(1) peek O(log n) O(log n) poll min-heap by comparator
ArrayDeque O(1) at both ends O(1) O(1) best stack and queue; no nulls
EnumMap / EnumSet O(1) O(1) O(1) array/bit-vector backed; very fast

Fail-fast vs weakly consistent iterators. ArrayList/HashMap iterators check a modCount; any structural modification not made through the iterator throws ConcurrentModificationException on the next next(). It's a best-effort bug detector, not a concurrency guarantee. Concurrent collections iterate over snapshots (CopyOnWriteArrayList) or are weakly consistent (ConcurrentHashMap) and never throw CME.

Java
// Removing while iterating
list.removeIf(Item::isExpired);                                  // best
for (Iterator<Item> it = list.iterator(); it.hasNext();)
    if (it.next().isExpired()) it.remove();                      // also correct
for (Item x : list) if (x.isExpired()) list.remove(x);           // throws ConcurrentModificationException

Comparable vs Comparator

Java
record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary) implements Comparable<Employee> {
    public int compareTo(Employee o) { return name.compareTo(o.name); }     // natural order: by name
}
List<Employee> sorted = employees.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
        .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())
        .thenComparing(Employee::name))
    .toList();

compareTo should be consistent with equals (return 0 exactly when equals is true), otherwise sorted sets/maps behave differently from hash-based ones: a TreeSet drops "duplicates" that equals considers different.

Immutable vs unmodifiable

Factory Behaviour
List.of(...), Set.of, Map.of (Java 9) truly immutable; reject nulls; Set.of/Map.of reject duplicates
List.copyOf(c) (Java 10) immutable copy (returns the same instance if already immutable)
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) read-only view: changes to the backing list show through
Stream.toList() (Java 16) unmodifiable list (allows nulls)
Arrays.asList(arr) fixed-size view over the array: set works, add throws

Choosing quickly: default to ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, ArrayDeque; LinkedHashMap when order matters; TreeMap for sorted/range queries; EnumMap/EnumSet for enum keys; PriorityQueue for top-K and schedulers; concurrent collections when shared across threads.

java-java8.tldr:
• Functional interfaces: Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier, UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator.
  • Streams are lazy: intermediate operations build the pipeline, the terminal operation runs it once.
  • Master groupingBy, partitioningBy, toMap (with a merge function) and flatMap.
  • Optional is a return type for "maybe absent"; use orElseGet for expensive defaults.
java-java8.body:
Java 8 added functional programming to Java: lambdas (anonymous functions), method references, functional interfaces, the Stream API, Optional, and default methods on interfaces.

Functional interfaces have exactly one abstract method, so a lambda can implement them:

Interface Signature Example
Function<T,R> T → R String::length
BiFunction<T,U,R> (T, U) → R (a, b) -> a + b
Predicate<T> T → boolean String::isBlank
Consumer<T> T → void System.out::println
Supplier<T> () → T ArrayList::new
UnaryOperator<T> T → T String::trim
BinaryOperator<T> (T, T) → T Integer::sum
Primitive variants IntFunction, ToLongFunction, IntPredicate… avoid boxing

Lambdas can capture only effectively final local variables (they capture the value; allowing mutation would create races and confusing semantics). They don't create a new scope for this, unlike anonymous classes.

Method reference kinds: static (Integer::parseInt), bound instance (System.out::println), unbound instance (String::toLowerCase, the first argument becomes the receiver), constructor (ArrayList::new).

How a stream pipeline runs

  • Intermediate operations are lazy: nothing runs until a terminal operation.
  • Elements flow one at a time through the stateless stages (filter → map for element 1, then element 2…) — loop fusion, not one pass per stage. Stateful stages (sorted, distinct) buffer.
  • Short-circuiting operations (limit, findFirst, anyMatch) stop early, so infinite streams (Stream.iterate, Stream.generate) work.
  • A stream can be consumed once.
Java
List<String> result = Stream.of("delta", "alpha", "charlie", "bravo")
    .filter(s -> { System.out.println("filter " + s); return s.length() == 5; })
    .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s.toUpperCase(); })
    .findFirst()                        // stops after the first match
    .stream().toList();
// filter delta, map delta  -> ["DELTA"]; the other elements are never touched

Collectors you must know

Java
record Order(String customer, String city, BigDecimal amount, List<String> items) {}

// Total revenue per city
Map<String, BigDecimal> revenueByCity = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::city,
             Collectors.reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Order::amount, BigDecimal::add)));

// Count per customer, sorted map
Map<String, Long> perCustomer = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));

// Top 3 customers by order count
List<String> top3 = perCustomer.entrySet().stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed())
    .limit(3).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();

// Distinct items across all orders (flatMap: 1 order -> N items)
Set<String> allItems = orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.items().stream()).collect(Collectors.toSet());

// Partition into big and small orders
Map<Boolean, List<Order>> split = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> o.amount().compareTo(new BigDecimal("1000")) > 0));

// toMap with a merge function (duplicate keys otherwise throw IllegalStateException)
Map<String, BigDecimal> maxPerCustomer = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Order::customer, Order::amount, BigDecimal::max));

// Statistics in one pass
IntSummaryStatistics stats = orders.stream().mapToInt(o -> o.items().size()).summaryStatistics();

// Joining
String names = orders.stream().map(Order::customer).distinct().collect(Collectors.joining(", "));

Frequently asked stream puzzles

Java
// First non-repeated character
Character firstUnique = s.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()))
    .entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey).findFirst().orElse(null);

// Second highest distinct salary
Optional<Integer> second = salaries.stream().distinct()
    .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).skip(1).findFirst();

// Word frequency
Map<String, Long> freq = Arrays.stream(text.toLowerCase().split("\\W+"))
    .filter(w -> !w.isBlank())
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w, Collectors.counting()));

// Find duplicates
Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
Set<Integer> dups = nums.stream().filter(n -> !seen.add(n)).collect(Collectors.toSet());

// Group anagrams
Map<String, List<String>> anagrams = words.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w.chars().sorted()
        .collect(StringBuilder::new, StringBuilder::appendCodePoint, StringBuilder::append).toString()));

(The "find duplicates" version uses a side-effecting HashSet; fine sequentially, wrong for parallel streams. A pure alternative: groupingBy(identity, counting()) then filter counts > 1.)

map vs flatMap: map transforms each element 1:1 (Stream<Order> → Stream<List<String>>); flatMap maps each element to a stream and concatenates them (Stream<Order> → Stream<String>).

Optional — a return type that says "this may be absent".

Java
String city = userRepo.findById(id)                 // Optional<User>
    .map(User::address)
    .map(Address::city)
    .filter(c -> !c.isBlank())
    .orElse("UNKNOWN");

User u = userRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(id));
Do Don't
return Optional from methods that may find nothing use it for fields, parameters or collection elements
orElseGet(() -> expensive()) for costly defaults orElse(expensive()) (always evaluates its argument)
map, flatMap, filter, ifPresentOrElse isPresent() + get() everywhere
return an empty collection instead of Optional<List<…>> Optional.of(null) (throws) — use ofNullable

Default and static interface methods let interfaces evolve without breaking implementers (Collection.stream(), Map.getOrDefault). If a class inherits the same default method from two interfaces, it must override it and can delegate explicitly with InterfaceName.super.method().

Pitfall exceptions inside lambdas: functional interfaces can't throw checked exceptions, so wrap them (UncheckedIOException) or use a small helper; don't swallow them silently.

java-modern.tldr:
• Records are immutable data carriers with generated equals/hashCode/toString.
  • Sealed hierarchies plus pattern-matching switch give exhaustive, compiler-checked branching.
  • Text blocks, var, switch expressions and sequenced collections remove boilerplate.
  • LTS releases to know: 11, 17, 21 (virtual threads) and 25 (scoped values).
java-modern.body:
What arrived when (the LTS releases are what companies run)

Version Headline features
9 Modules (JPMS), List.of/Map.of, JShell, private interface methods, Optional.ifPresentOrElse
10 var local type inference, container awareness
11 (LTS) HttpClient, String.isBlank/strip/lines/repeat, Files.readString, single-file java Main.java
14 switch expressions (final), helpful NullPointerException messages
15 text blocks, ZGC/Shenandoah production-ready
16 records, instanceof pattern matching, Stream.toList()
17 (LTS) sealed classes, strong encapsulation of JDK internals
21 (LTS) virtual threads, record patterns, pattern matching for switch, sequenced collections, generational ZGC
22–24 unnamed variables _, stream gatherers, FFM API, synchronized no longer pins virtual threads (24)
25 (LTS) scoped values, compact source files and instance main, module imports, flexible constructor bodies

Records — transparent, immutable data carriers. The compiler generates the canonical constructor, accessors (x(), not getX()), equals, hashCode and toString.

Java
public record Point(int x, int y) {
    public Point {                                   // compact constructor: validation / normalization
        if (x < 0 || y < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative");
    }
    public Point withX(int nx) { return new Point(nx, y); }   // "wither" for immutable updates
    public static Point origin() { return new Point(0, 0); }
}

Records can implement interfaces and have static members and extra methods, but can't extend classes or declare instance fields beyond their components. They're shallowly immutable: a List component is still mutable unless you copy it (List.copyOf in the compact constructor). Ideal for DTOs, value objects, map keys, events and results.

Sealed types + pattern matching — model a closed set of alternatives and let the compiler check you handled them all.

Java
public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Rect {}
public record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
public record Square(double side) implements Shape {}
public record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape {}

static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {                                        // exhaustive: no default needed
        case Circle c                  -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
        case Square(double a)          -> a * a;               // record deconstruction pattern (21)
        case Rect(double w, double h) when w == h -> w * w;    // guard
        case Rect(double w, double h)  -> w * h;
    };
}

Add a new Triangle to permits and every non-exhaustive switch becomes a compile error — the opposite of a forgotten else branch at runtime. This is how modern Java models results (sealed interface PaymentResult permits Approved, Declined, Pending) and domain events.

Pattern matching for instanceof

Java
if (obj instanceof String s && !s.isBlank()) {       // s is in scope where the match is definitely true
    System.out.println(s.length());
}

Switch expressions return values, use -> (no fall-through), and must be exhaustive:

Java
int days = switch (month) {
    case FEBRUARY -> leap ? 29 : 28;
    case APRIL, JUNE, SEPTEMBER, NOVEMBER -> 30;
    default -> 31;
};

Text blocks

Java
String json = """
    {
      "id": %d,
      "name": "%s"
    }
    """.formatted(id, name);      // indentation is stripped relative to the closing delimiter

var infers local variable types: great for long generic types (var map = new HashMap<String, List<Order>>()), bad when it hides an important type (var x = service.process()). Only for locals, not fields or parameters.

Sequenced collections (21) give a uniform API for collections with an order:

Java
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
list.getFirst(); list.getLast(); list.reversed();         // also on Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap (firstEntry...)

Other modern features worth naming: HttpClient (HTTP/2, async); helpful NPE messages (Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "user.name" is null); unnamed variables (catch (Exception _), case Point(var x, _)); stream gatherers (custom intermediate operations, JDK 24); the Foreign Function & Memory API replacing JNI (JDK 22).

Interview tip when asked "which Java version do you use and what do you like in it?", talk about records + sealed types + switch patterns for domain modelling, and virtual threads for I/O-heavy services — and mention you'd upgrade LTS to LTS (17 → 21 → 25).

java-exceptions.tldr:
• Checked exceptions are for recoverable conditions; unchecked for bugs and most business failures.
  • try-with-resources closes in reverse order and keeps close() failures as suppressed exceptions.
  • Never return from finally; never swallow exceptions; wrap with context and keep the cause.
  • Map domain exceptions to responses in one global handler.
java-exceptions.body:
Kind Compiler forces handling? Meaning Examples
Checked yes: catch or declare throws recoverable condition outside the program's control IOException, SQLException, InterruptedException
Unchecked (RuntimeException) no programming errors, or business failures callers usually can't fix locally IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, domain exceptions
Error no serious JVM-level problems; don't catch except to log and exit OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError

Modern frameworks (Spring, JPA, Jackson) mostly throw unchecked exceptions and translate checked ones (SQLException → Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy), because checked exceptions leak implementation details through every method signature and don't compose with lambdas.

How try / catch / finally executes

finally runs whether the try completes normally, returns, or throws — except when the JVM halts (System.exit, crash, kill -9) or the thread is a daemon at JVM exit.

try-with-resources closes resources in reverse order of declaration, even if the body throws, and keeps the original exception as primary while attaching any close() failures as suppressed exceptions (e.getSuppressed()).

Java
try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(SQL)) {     // closed first
    ps.setLong(1, id);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) { /* ... */ }
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new DataAccessFailure("load user " + id, e);        // wrap with context, KEEP the cause
}

Any class implementing AutoCloseable works in try-with-resources — including your own (locks released, metrics timers stopped, temp files deleted).

final vs finally vs finalize

Keyword Meaning
final variable can't be reassigned; method can't be overridden; class can't be extended
finally block that always runs after try/catch
finalize() old GC callback; unpredictable, deprecated for removal (JDK 18). Use try-with-resources or java.lang.ref.Cleaner

Traps interviewers love

Java
// 1. return in finally overrides the try's return AND swallows exceptions
int f() { try { throw new IllegalStateException(); } finally { return 1; } }   // returns 1, exception lost

// 2. finally runs after the return value is computed
int g() { int x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 2; } }                       // returns 1

// 3. Catch order: specific before general (otherwise: compile error "exception already caught")
try { readFile(); }
catch (FileNotFoundException e) { /* specific */ }
catch (IOException e) { /* general */ }

// 4. Multi-catch for identical handling
catch (JsonProcessingException | DateTimeParseException e) { throw new BadRequestException(e.getMessage(), e); }

Designing exceptions for a service

Java
// A small domain hierarchy: stable codes, mapped centrally to HTTP responses
public abstract class DomainException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String code;
    protected DomainException(String code, String message) { super(message); this.code = code; }
    public String code() { return code; }
}
public class OrderNotFoundException extends DomainException {
    public OrderNotFoundException(long id) { super("order_not_found", "Order " + id + " not found"); }
}
public class InsufficientStockException extends DomainException {
    public InsufficientStockException(String sku, int requested, int available) {
        super("insufficient_stock", "Requested " + requested + " of " + sku + " but only " + available + " left");
    }
}
// @RestControllerAdvice maps DomainException subclasses to 404/409/422 with ProblemDetail (see API Design → errors)

Best practices

  • Catch the most specific type you can handle; let the rest propagate to one global handler.
  • Never swallow: catch (Exception e) {} hides bugs forever. If you truly ignore an exception, comment why.
  • Log or rethrow, not both at every layer — otherwise one failure produces five stack traces.
  • Keep the cause when wrapping (new X("context", e)), and add context (ids, parameters) to the message.
  • Don't use exceptions for normal control flow (they're expensive to create because they capture the stack trace).
  • Restore the interrupt flag when catching InterruptedException.
  • Fail fast on invalid input with IllegalArgumentException / Objects.requireNonNull at boundaries.

Pitfall catching Throwable or Error (e.g. to "keep the loop alive") can continue running in a corrupted state after OutOfMemoryError or StackOverflowError. Let the JVM die (-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError) and let the orchestrator restart it.

java-generics.tldr:
• Generics are erased at runtime: no new T(), no T.class, no instanceof List<String>.
  • PECS: producer extends, consumer super.
  • Generics are invariant (List<Object> isn't a supertype of List<String>); arrays are covariant.
  • Keep runtime types with Class tokens or super-type tokens.
java-generics.body:
Generics give compile-time type safety for containers and algorithms: List<String> rejects an Integer at compile time and removes casts from your code.

Type erasure. Generic type information exists only at compile time. The compiler checks types, then erases type parameters to their bounds (or Object) and inserts casts in the bytecode.

Consequences of erasure:

You can't… Because Workaround
new T() or new T[n] T is unknown at runtime pass a Supplier<T> or Class<T>
obj instanceof List<String> runtime only sees List instanceof List<?> and check elements
overload m(List<String>) and m(List<Integer>) both erase to m(List) different method names
use primitives as type arguments type arguments must be reference types boxed types, or primitive specializations (IntStream)
create generic arrays safely arrays need their component type at runtime use List<T>
catch a generic exception type erased —

Invariance. List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>, even though String is a subtype of Object. If it were, you could add an Integer through the List<Object> reference into a list of strings. Arrays are covariant, which is exactly the hole generics close:

Java
Object[] objs = new String[1];
objs[0] = 42;                  // compiles, then throws ArrayStoreException at runtime

List<Object> list = new ArrayList<String>();   // does NOT compile: generics catch it early

Wildcards and PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super

Wildcard You can read as You can write Use when the parameter…
List<? extends T> T nothing (except null) produces values for you (Producer Extends)
List<? super T> Object T and its subtypes consumes values from you (Consumer Super)
List<?> Object nothing you only use Object methods / size
List<T> T T you both read and write
Java
// Reads from src (producer) -> extends; writes to dst (consumer) -> super
public static <T> void copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst) {
    for (T item : src) dst.add(item);
}

double sum(Collection<? extends Number> nums) {           // works for List<Integer>, Set<Double>...
    return nums.stream().mapToDouble(Number::doubleValue).sum();
}

// Bounded type parameter; "? super T" lets it work for types whose Comparable is declared on a supertype
public static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(List<? extends T> list) {
    return list.stream().max(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow();
}

Collections.sort(List<T> list, Comparator<? super T> c) is PECS in the JDK: a Comparator<Object> can sort a List<String>.

Generic methods and inference

Java
public static <K, V> Map<V, K> invert(Map<K, V> m) {
    Map<V, K> out = new HashMap<>();
    m.forEach((k, v) -> out.put(v, k));
    return out;
}
Map<Integer, String> byId = invert(Map.of("nk", 1, "asha", 2));   // K and V inferred

Keeping types at runtime — pass a type token:

Java
<T> T read(String json, Class<T> type) { return mapper.readValue(json, type); }
// For generic types use a super-type token, which captures the type in a subclass's signature:
List<Order> orders = mapper.readValue(json, new TypeReference<List<Order>>() {});   // Jackson
ResponseEntity<List<Order>> res = rest.exchange(url, HttpMethod.GET, null,
        new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<Order>>() {});                         // Spring

Raw types (List without a type argument) exist only for pre-Java-5 compatibility; they disable type checking and produce unchecked warnings. Don't use them in new code.

Heap pollution and @SafeVarargs. Generic varargs (List<String>... lists) create a generic array under the hood, which can be corrupted; annotate methods that don't misuse the array with @SafeVarargs.

java-jvm.tldr:
• Runtime areas: heap (young/old), Metaspace, per-thread stacks, PC registers, code cache.
  • Class loaders delegate to their parent first (Application → Platform → Bootstrap).
  • Code starts interpreted; hot methods get JIT-compiled by C1 then C2 with inlining and escape analysis.
  • Know jcmd for heap info, dumps, thread dumps and Flight Recorder.
java-jvm.body:
Runtime data areas

Area Shared? Holds Error when exhausted Sized by
Heap all threads objects, arrays, interned strings OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space -Xmx, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage
Metaspace all threads class metadata OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize (unbounded by default)
Code cache all threads compiled code JIT stops compiling (performance drops) -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize
JVM stack per thread frames: locals, partial results StackOverflowError -Xss
PC register per thread address of the current instruction — —
Direct memory all threads NIO direct buffers OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize

A stack frame in action

Java
int add(int a, int b) { int sum = a + b; return sum; }
// Frame for add(): local variables [this, a, b, sum]; the operand stack holds a and b,
// iadd pops both and pushes the result, istore saves it into `sum`.
// Deep or infinite recursion keeps pushing frames until StackOverflowError.

Class loading: load → link → initialize

Initialization happens on first active use (creating an instance, calling a static method, reading a non-constant static field) and is thread-safe: the JVM locks the class while initializing it. That's why the holder-class singleton idiom is lazy and safe without any locking.

Class loader hierarchy and parent delegation

A loader first asks its parent; only if the parent can't find the class does it load it itself. This guarantees core classes like java.lang.String always come from the JDK (you can't shadow them) and each class is loaded once per loader. A class's identity is (name + defining loader): the same class loaded by two loaders is two different types, which causes the famous ClassCastException: com.x.Foo cannot be cast to com.x.Foo in app servers and plugin systems. Tomcat deliberately inverts delegation per web app (child-first) for isolation.

Execution engine: interpreter + tiered JIT

C2 optimizations worth naming: inlining (the most important), escape analysis (objects that never escape a method are scalar-replaced, i.e. not allocated on the heap at all, and their locks elided), loop unrolling, null-check and bounds-check elimination, and speculative devirtualization of interface calls based on observed types. This is why Java "warms up": the first requests run interpreted and slow; JIT-compiled code is fast. GraalVM can replace C2 (-XX:+UseJVMCICompiler) or compile ahead of time (native image).

Useful flags and tools

Shell
java -Xms2g -Xmx2g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
     -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime -jar app.jar
# Containers: prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 (the JVM is container-aware since JDK 10)

jcmd <pid> VM.flags                 # effective flags
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info             # heap summary
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram       # objects per class
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/h.hprof
jcmd <pid> Thread.print             # thread dump
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr   # Flight Recorder profiling
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000            # GC utilization every second
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -i heapsize

java-gc.tldr:
• Objects are live if reachable from GC roots; most die young, so generational collection pays off.
  • G1 is the default (region-based, pause target); ZGC gives sub-millisecond pauses; Parallel maximizes throughput.
  • Soft, weak and phantom references serve caches, canonical maps and cleanup.
  • Java leaks are reachable-but-unneeded objects; find them with a heap dump and the dominator tree.
java-gc.body:
The garbage collector frees memory occupied by objects the program can no longer reach.

Reachability, not reference counting. An object is live if it can be reached from a GC root by following references. Everything else is garbage, including cycles of objects that only reference each other.

Here Session and Cart reference each other but nothing reachable references them, so both are collected. GC roots include: local variables and operands on thread stacks, static fields of loaded classes, JNI references, active monitors, and threads themselves.

Generational hypothesis: most objects die young. So the heap is split, and the young generation is collected often and cheaply.

  • Minor GC: Eden fills → live objects are copied to a survivor space (or promoted); Eden is wiped in one go. Cost is proportional to live objects, so mostly-garbage young gens are cheap.
  • Objects surviving several minor GCs are promoted to the old generation.
  • Old-gen collection is more expensive because more data is live.

Core algorithms

Algorithm How Trade-off
Mark–sweep mark live objects, free the rest in place fragmentation
Mark–compact mark, then slide live objects together no fragmentation; moving costs time
Copying copy live objects to an empty space fast when few survive; needs spare space (young gen)

Stop-the-world vs concurrent. Some phases must pause all application threads at a safepoint; modern collectors do most marking (and ZGC/Shenandoah even compaction) concurrently with the application, using read/write barriers to keep track of changes.

The collectors

Collector Flag Profile Use when
Serial -XX:+UseSerialGC single-threaded, stop-the-world tiny heaps, 1-CPU containers
Parallel -XX:+UseParallelGC multi-threaded STW, maximum throughput batch jobs where pauses don't matter
G1 (default since 9) -XX:+UseG1GC region-based, pause-time goal, concurrent marking most services
ZGC -XX:+UseZGC (generational by default from JDK 23; -XX:+ZGenerational on 21) concurrent compaction, sub-millisecond pauses, heaps up to TBs latency-critical services, big heaps
Shenandoah -XX:+UseShenandoahGC concurrent compaction, low pauses similar to ZGC (Red Hat builds)

How G1 works

The heap is split into ~2048 equal regions (1–32 MB each). Any region can play any role, and the roles change over time; a humongous object (≥ half a region) gets contiguous regions of its own.

  1. Young collections (STW): evacuate live objects from Eden/Survivor regions into new regions.
  2. When old-gen occupancy passes InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (adaptive, starts at 45%), a concurrent marking cycle finds how much live data each old region has.
  3. Mixed collections then evacuate young regions plus the old regions with the most garbage first (hence "Garbage-First"), choosing how many to fit the pause goal (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, default 200 ms).
  4. If concurrent work can't keep up, G1 falls back to a full GC (STW compaction of the whole heap) — the thing you want to never see.

Reference types

Type Cleared when Use
Strong never while reachable normal references
Soft (SoftReference) only under memory pressure memory-sensitive caches (prefer a bounded Caffeine cache instead)
Weak (WeakReference) at the next GC once only weakly reachable canonicalizing maps (WeakHashMap), ThreadLocal keys, listener registries
Phantom (PhantomReference) after finalization; get() always returns null post-mortem cleanup (Cleaner)

Memory leaks in Java are objects that are still reachable but no longer needed: growing static collections, unbounded caches, listeners never removed, ThreadLocals on pooled threads, non-static inner classes holding their outer instance, and keys with changing hash codes. Find them with a heap dump and the dominator tree (Production Debugging → memory leak).

Tuning, in the right order

  1. Measure: GC logs (-Xlog:gc*), pause metrics (jvm_gc_pause_seconds), allocation profiling (JFR).
  2. Reduce allocation and live data in the code (often the biggest win).
  3. Give the heap headroom (G1 needs free regions); set -Xms = -Xmx for steady services.
  4. Set a realistic pause goal; switch to ZGC if you need consistently tiny pauses.
  5. Change one flag at a time and load-test.

Interview tip "How does GC know what to free?" → reachability from GC roots via tracing, not reference counting, so cycles are collected. "Why generations?" → most objects die young, so collecting the young gen often is cheap because cost scales with live objects, not garbage.

java-patterns.tldr:
• SOLID: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
  • Strategy replaces if/else chains; Spring can inject every implementation into a map by type.
  • Builder for many optional parameters; Factory for creation by type; Observer, Decorator and Proxy appear throughout Spring.
  • Use patterns where variation exists, not for decoration.
java-patterns.body:
SOLID

Principle Meaning Smell when violated Fix
Single responsibility one reason to change InvoiceService that calculates, renders PDFs and emails split into InvoiceCalculator, InvoicePdfRenderer, InvoiceMailer
Open/closed extend by adding code, not editing it a growing switch (type) in many places polymorphism / strategy
Liskov substitution subtypes honor the parent's contract Square extends Rectangle breaks setWidth; subclasses throwing UnsupportedOperationException separate types, composition
Interface segregation small, focused interfaces implementers stubbing methods they don't need split the interface
Dependency inversion depend on abstractions; inject implementations new MySqlOrderRepository() inside a service constructor injection of an interface (Spring DI)

Pattern map: which problem each solves

Family Pattern Problem it solves Where you see it
Creational Factory method / static factory create by type without exposing classes List.of, Executors.newFixedThreadPool
Builder many optional parameters, immutable result HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Lombok @Builder
Singleton one shared instance Spring singleton beans (via DI, not the GoF pattern)
Prototype copy existing objects clone(), Spring prototype scope
Structural Adapter make one interface fit another Arrays.asList, InputStreamReader
Decorator add behaviour by wrapping BufferedInputStream, Spring TaskDecorator
Proxy control access / add cross-cutting logic Spring AOP, @Transactional, JPA lazy loading
Facade simple API over a complex subsystem JdbcTemplate
Composite treat trees of objects uniformly UI components, rule engines
Behavioural Strategy interchangeable algorithms Comparator, pricing/payment strategies
Template method fixed skeleton, variable steps AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, JdbcTemplate callbacks
Observer notify subscribers of changes Spring ApplicationEvent, listeners
Chain of responsibility pass a request along handlers servlet filters, Spring Security filter chain
Command encapsulate a request as an object Runnable tasks, undo/redo
State behaviour depends on internal state order/booking lifecycles, vending machine
Iterator traverse without exposing structure Iterator, streams

Strategy — removes if/else chains; Spring injects every implementation:

Java
public interface PaymentStrategy {
    PaymentType type();
    Receipt pay(Order order);
}
@Component class UpiPayment implements PaymentStrategy { /* type() = UPI */ }
@Component class CardPayment implements PaymentStrategy { /* type() = CARD */ }

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    private final Map<PaymentType, PaymentStrategy> strategies;
    public PaymentService(List<PaymentStrategy> all) {                    // Spring injects every implementation
        this.strategies = all.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(PaymentStrategy::type, s -> s));
    }
    public Receipt pay(Order o) {
        PaymentStrategy s = strategies.get(o.paymentType());
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unsupported payment type " + o.paymentType());
        return s.pay(o);
    }
}
// Adding NetBanking = one new @Component class; PaymentService never changes (open/closed).

Builder — many optional parameters, immutable result, readable call sites:

Java
public final class HttpRequestSpec {
    private final String url; private final String method; private final Duration timeout; private final Map<String, String> headers;
    private HttpRequestSpec(Builder b) { url = b.url; method = b.method; timeout = b.timeout; headers = Map.copyOf(b.headers); }
    public static Builder builder(String url) { return new Builder(url); }

    public static final class Builder {
        private final String url; private String method = "GET"; private Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(5);
        private final Map<String, String> headers = new HashMap<>();
        private Builder(String url) { this.url = Objects.requireNonNull(url); }
        public Builder method(String m) { this.method = m; return this; }
        public Builder timeout(Duration t) { this.timeout = t; return this; }
        public Builder header(String k, String v) { headers.put(k, v); return this; }
        public HttpRequestSpec build() {                                    // validate once, at the end
            if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("timeout");
            return new HttpRequestSpec(this);
        }
    }
}
HttpRequestSpec req = HttpRequestSpec.builder("https://api").method("POST").timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).header("X-Id", "1").build();

Decorator — wrap to add behaviour without subclassing:

Java
public interface Notifier { void send(String to, String msg); }
public class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { public void send(String to, String msg) { /* SMTP */ } }

public class RetryingNotifier implements Notifier {                 // decorator
    private final Notifier inner; private final int attempts;
    public RetryingNotifier(Notifier inner, int attempts) { this.inner = inner; this.attempts = attempts; }
    public void send(String to, String msg) {
        for (int i = 1; ; i++) {
            try { inner.send(to, msg); return; }
            catch (RuntimeException e) { if (i == attempts) throw e; }
        }
    }
}
Notifier n = new RetryingNotifier(new LoggingNotifier(new EmailNotifier()), 3);   // stackable

Observer in Spring — decouple "something happened" from "what reacts":

Java
public record OrderPlaced(long orderId) {}

@Service class OrderService {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
    OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher events) { this.events = events; }
    @Transactional public void place(Order o) { /* save */ events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(o.getId())); }
}
@Component class EmailOnOrder {
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)    // only if the order really committed
    void on(OrderPlaced e) { /* send email */ }
}

Interview tip name the problem first ("the variation here is the pricing rule, so Strategy"), never the pattern first. Over-patterned code (factories for one class, interfaces with one implementation forever) is its own smell.

java-misc.tldr:
• Declare serialVersionUID; avoid Java serialization for untrusted data — prefer JSON/Protobuf.
  • clone() is shallow; prefer copy constructors.
  • Integer caches −128..127, so compare wrappers with equals.
  • Use BigDecimal from strings for money and compare with compareTo.
java-misc.body:
Serialization

  • Implementing Serializable lets ObjectOutputStream write an object graph to bytes. Fields marked transient and static fields are skipped.
  • Declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; explicitly. Otherwise the JVM computes one from the class structure, so recompiling after a harmless change makes old data fail with InvalidClassException.
  • Custom control: writeObject/readObject, writeReplace/readResolve (keeps singletons singletons), or Externalizable.
  • Security: deserializing untrusted bytes with Java serialization can execute attacker-chosen code through "gadget chains" in your classpath. Never accept Java-serialized data from outside; if you must, use an ObjectInputFilter allowlist. For data exchange use JSON, Protobuf or Avro.

Cloning: shallow vs deep

Object.clone() (with Cloneable) is shallow by default and has a famously awkward contract (no constructor call, CloneNotSupportedException, final fields can't be reassigned). Prefer copy constructors or static factories: new Order(other), List.copyOf(...), or immutable objects that never need copying.

Reflection inspects and invokes classes at runtime: getDeclaredFields(), getMethod(...).invoke(...), setAccessible(true), annotations. It powers Spring DI, Jackson, JPA/Hibernate, JUnit and Mockito.

  • Costs: slower than direct calls (much improved by MethodHandle-based reflection in JDK 18), bypasses compile-time checks, breaks encapsulation.
  • Since JDK 16/17, deep reflection into JDK internals is blocked by strong encapsulation unless opened with --add-opens.
  • MethodHandle/VarHandle are the faster, type-checked alternatives for frameworks.
Java
record Customer(String name, int tier) {}
for (RecordComponent rc : Customer.class.getRecordComponents()) {
    System.out.println(rc.getName() + " = " + rc.getAccessor().invoke(new Customer("nk", 2)));   // name = nk, tier = 2
}

static

On Meaning
field one copy per class, shared by all instances
method belongs to the class; can't use this or instance members; can't be overridden (only hidden)
block runs once at class initialization, in source order
nested class doesn't hold a reference to an outer instance

Pitfall a non-static inner class (and anonymous class or lambda capturing this) holds a hidden reference to its outer instance. Storing one in a long-lived place (a static cache, a listener list) keeps the whole outer object alive — a classic leak.

Wrapper caching and autoboxing

Java
Integer a = 127, b = 127;
System.out.println(a == b);        // true: Integer.valueOf caches -128..127
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(c == d);        // false: different objects
System.out.println(c.equals(d));   // true

Integer missing = null;
int x = missing;                   // NullPointerException on auto-unboxing
Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>();
int count = m.get("absent");       // NPE: get returns null, unboxing fails

Always compare wrappers with equals; avoid boxed types in hot loops (allocation and cache misses).

Money and floating point

Java
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);                            // 0.30000000000000004
BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("0.1"), b = new BigDecimal("0.2");
System.out.println(a.add(b));                             // 0.3
System.out.println(new BigDecimal(0.1));                  // 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827... (from a double!)
System.out.println(new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")));        // false: scale differs
System.out.println(new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00")));     // 0: numerically equal
BigDecimal perPerson = new BigDecimal("100").divide(new BigDecimal("3"), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);   // 33.33

Construct BigDecimal from strings (or BigDecimal.valueOf(double)), always specify a scale and RoundingMode when dividing (otherwise non-terminating results throw ArithmeticException), compare with compareTo, or store integer minor units (paise) in a long.

Other classics, quickly

Question Answer
== vs equals reference identity vs logical equality
Can you override a static method? no, it's hidden; calls resolve by static type
Why is main static? the JVM calls it without creating an instance (JDK 25 also allows instance main in compact source files)
transient vs volatile skip in serialization vs cross-thread visibility
Checked exception in an overriding method can't be broader than the parent's
Marker interfaces Serializable, Cloneable: no methods, just a tag (annotations are the modern alternative)
String in switch uses hashCode then equals
Integer overflow silent wraparound; use Math.addExact to throw instead

qa.q: Why is String immutable in Java?
qa.a: Security (class names, URLs and file paths can't be changed after validation), thread safety without synchronization, hash code caching (fast HashMap keys), and it enables the string pool where many references share one object.

qa.q: Explain how HashMap works internally.
qa.a: It stores entries in an array of buckets. put computes hash(key) (spreading high bits), finds index hash & (n-1), and inserts into that bucket's list (or tree). On collision it compares with equals. Bins with ≥ 8 nodes treeify (if capacity ≥ 64). When size exceeds capacity × load factor (0.75) the table doubles and entries are redistributed. get follows the same path. Average O(1), worst O(log n) with treeified bins.

qa.q: What happens if two keys have the same hashCode?
qa.a: They go to the same bucket (collision). HashMap distinguishes them with equals. If equals is also true, the second put replaces the value. Many collisions degrade performance, which is why bins treeify.

qa.q: Difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
qa.a: ArrayList is a resizable array: O(1) random access, amortized O(1) append, O(n) inserts in the middle, compact and cache-friendly. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: O(n) access, O(1) insert/remove at a known node, high memory overhead per element. In practice ArrayList (or ArrayDeque for queues) wins almost always.

qa.q: HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap vs SynchronizedMap?
qa.a: HashMap: not thread-safe, allows one null key and null values. Hashtable: legacy, every method synchronized on one lock, no nulls. Collections.synchronizedMap: wrapper with one lock; iteration needs manual synchronization. ConcurrentHashMap: fine-grained (per-bin) locking, lock-free reads, atomic compound ops, no nulls. Use HashMap single-threaded and ConcurrentHashMap concurrently.

qa.q: How do you make a class immutable?
qa.a: Make the class final; all fields private final; no setters; initialize everything in the constructor; defensively copy mutable inputs and never expose mutable internals (return copies or unmodifiable views); don't let this escape during construction. Or use a record with immutable component types.

qa.q: What is the difference between == and equals()?
qa.a: == compares references for objects (and values for primitives). equals compares logical equality as defined by the class; Object.equals defaults to ==. Strings, wrappers and collections override equals.

qa.q: Checked vs unchecked exceptions — which do you prefer?
qa.a: Checked exceptions are enforced by the compiler and suit recoverable, expected conditions. Unchecked ones signal bugs or conditions callers usually can't recover from. Modern frameworks (Spring) translate checked exceptions into unchecked ones to avoid throws clutter; I use unchecked domain exceptions and handle them centrally.

qa.q: What is the difference between map and flatMap in streams?
qa.a: map applies a one-to-one function. flatMap applies a function returning a stream for each element and flattens the results into one stream, e.g. turning List<Order> into a stream of all line items.

qa.q: Are streams faster than loops?
qa.a: Not inherently; sequential streams add slight overhead. They win on readability and composability. Parallel streams can help for large CPU-bound workloads on splittable sources, but run on the shared common pool and are slower for small data or I/O.

qa.q: What are intermediate vs terminal operations? Why is laziness useful?
qa.a: Intermediate ops build the pipeline and return a stream; terminal ops trigger execution. Laziness enables short-circuiting (findFirst, limit, anyMatch stop early), fuses operations into a single pass and allows infinite streams (Stream.iterate).

qa.q: What are the memory areas in the JVM?
qa.a: Heap (young + old; objects), Metaspace (class metadata, native memory), per-thread JVM stacks (frames, locals), PC registers, native method stacks, and the code cache for JIT-compiled code.

qa.q: Difference between StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError?
qa.a: StackOverflowError: a thread's stack is exhausted, typically from infinite or too-deep recursion. OutOfMemoryError: the heap (or Metaspace, or native memory for threads, or direct buffers) can't satisfy an allocation even after GC.

qa.q: How does garbage collection work? Which GC would you choose?
qa.a: GC traces reachable objects from roots and reclaims the rest; generational collectors collect the young gen often and cheaply, and the old gen rarely. G1 is the default and a good balance with pause-time targets. Choose ZGC for large heaps and strict latency SLAs, Parallel for throughput-oriented batch jobs. Decide with GC logs and load tests, not guesses.

qa.q: Can a Java application have memory leaks? Give examples.
qa.a: Yes: objects that stay reachable but are unused. Growing static maps, unbounded caches, listeners never unregistered, ThreadLocals in pooled threads, non-static inner classes holding outer instances, and keys whose hashCode changes. Diagnose with heap dumps and the dominator tree.

qa.q: What is the volatile vs transient keyword?
qa.a: volatile concerns concurrency: visibility and ordering of a field across threads. transient concerns serialization: the field is skipped when serializing.

qa.q: What are records and when would you use them?
qa.a: Records (Java 16) are concise immutable data carriers: the compiler generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. Use them for DTOs, value objects, map keys and event payloads. They can't extend classes, and fields are final.

qa.q: What are sealed classes for?
qa.a: They restrict which classes may extend or implement a type (permits). The compiler then knows all subtypes, enabling exhaustive switch pattern matching without a default, which is ideal for modelling closed domain hierarchies like payment results or events.

qa.q: Explain Comparable vs Comparator.
qa.a: Comparable is implemented by the class itself (compareTo) to define one natural order. Comparator is a separate object defining any number of orderings, composable with comparing, thenComparing and reversed.

qa.q: What is the diamond problem and how does Java handle it?
qa.a: A class inheriting the same method from two parents. Java forbids multiple class inheritance; with interfaces' default methods, if two interfaces provide the same default, the implementing class must override it and can delegate with InterfaceName.super.method().

qa.q: What is type erasure?
qa.a: Generic type information exists only at compile time; the compiler inserts casts and erases type parameters to their bounds (or Object) in bytecode. Hence no new T(), no instanceof List<String>, and no overloads differing only by type argument.

qa.q: Why should you override hashCode when overriding equals?
qa.a: Hash-based collections first locate the bucket by hashCode, then compare with equals. If equal objects have different hash codes, a lookup searches the wrong bucket and never finds the entry, breaking HashMap/HashSet semantics.

qa.q: Explain the class loading delegation model.
qa.a: When asked to load a class, a loader first delegates to its parent (Application → Platform → Bootstrap). Only if the parent can't find it does the child load it. This prevents user code from replacing core classes and ensures each class is loaded once per loader. Frameworks like Tomcat deliberately invert it per web app for isolation.

qa.q: What is a functional interface? Can you write a custom one?
qa.a: An interface with exactly one abstract method (default and static methods allowed), usable as a lambda target. Annotate with @FunctionalInterface so the compiler enforces it, e.g. @FunctionalInterface interface Validator<T> { boolean validate(T t); }.

cheat.java-cheatsheet:
OOP and the object contract

  • Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism (overloading at compile time, overriding at runtime).
  • Equal objects must have equal hash codes: override equals and hashCode together, or use a record.
  • Abstract classes share state and code; interfaces define capabilities and allow multiple inheritance.
  • Java is always pass-by-value; for objects the reference is copied. Prefer composition over inheritance.

Strings, immutability and the string pool

  • Strings are immutable: thread-safe, cacheable hash codes, safe keys, and they enable the string pool.
  • == compares references; equals compares content; intern() returns the pooled copy.
  • Use StringBuilder for concatenation in loops; StringBuffer is the legacy synchronized version.
  • Keep passwords in char[] so they can be cleared.

Collections framework and HashMap internals

  • HashMap: spread hash, bucket by hash & (n-1), chain collisions, treeify at 8 when capacity ≥ 64, resize at 0.75 load.
  • ArrayList beats LinkedList almost always; ArrayDeque is the best stack/queue.
  • Fail-fast iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException; remove with removeIf or the iterator.
  • List.of is immutable; Collections.unmodifiableList is only a read-only view.

Java 8: lambdas, functional interfaces, streams, Optional

  • Functional interfaces: Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier, UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator.
  • Streams are lazy: intermediate operations build the pipeline, the terminal operation runs it once.
  • Master groupingBy, partitioningBy, toMap (with a merge function) and flatMap.
  • Optional is a return type for "maybe absent"; use orElseGet for expensive defaults.

Java 9–25: records, sealed types, pattern matching, text blocks

  • Records are immutable data carriers with generated equals/hashCode/toString.
  • Sealed hierarchies plus pattern-matching switch give exhaustive, compiler-checked branching.
  • Text blocks, var, switch expressions and sequenced collections remove boilerplate.
  • LTS releases to know: 11, 17, 21 (virtual threads) and 25 (scoped values).

Exceptions and error handling

  • Checked exceptions are for recoverable conditions; unchecked for bugs and most business failures.
  • try-with-resources closes in reverse order and keeps close() failures as suppressed exceptions.
  • Never return from finally; never swallow exceptions; wrap with context and keep the cause.
  • Map domain exceptions to responses in one global handler.

Generics, type erasure and wildcards

  • Generics are erased at runtime: no new T(), no T.class, no instanceof List<String>.
  • PECS: producer extends, consumer super.
  • Generics are invariant (List<Object> isn't a supertype of List<String>); arrays are covariant.
  • Keep runtime types with Class tokens or super-type tokens.

JVM architecture, memory areas and class loading

  • Runtime areas: heap (young/old), Metaspace, per-thread stacks, PC registers, code cache.
  • Class loaders delegate to their parent first (Application → Platform → Bootstrap).
  • Code starts interpreted; hot methods get JIT-compiled by C1 then C2 with inlining and escape analysis.
  • Know jcmd for heap info, dumps, thread dumps and Flight Recorder.

Garbage collection

  • Objects are live if reachable from GC roots; most die young, so generational collection pays off.
  • G1 is the default (region-based, pause target); ZGC gives sub-millisecond pauses; Parallel maximizes throughput.
  • Soft, weak and phantom references serve caches, canonical maps and cleanup.
  • Java leaks are reachable-but-unneeded objects; find them with a heap dump and the dominator tree.

Design patterns and SOLID with Java examples

  • SOLID: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
  • Strategy replaces if/else chains; Spring can inject every implementation into a map by type.
  • Builder for many optional parameters; Factory for creation by type; Observer, Decorator and Proxy appear throughout Spring.
  • Use patterns where variation exists, not for decoration.

Serialization, cloning, reflection and other classics

  • Declare serialVersionUID; avoid Java serialization for untrusted data — prefer JSON/Protobuf.
  • clone() is shallow; prefer copy constructors.
  • Integer caches −128..127, so compare wrappers with equals.
  • Use BigDecimal from strings for money and compare with compareTo.
